chapter_theme: A song at Kurudimalai (குருடிமலை): the poet says he cannot understand the ways of poets who flatter men of the world as Vishnu and patch together stolen verses for the ignorant; the praise is of the flooding river at the hill.

613.reading: The poet describes poets who cry out praising worldly men as the dark cloud riding on Garuda or a lotus jewel, slip their names into their verses, hunt through old sayings, steal and knead a measure of them, and sing poems that enter only the ears of the ignorant, and says he does not know how to grasp even a little of what such poets say. The praise pictures the river called Madhuram flooding both banks and toppling agil and marutham trees where wild goats graze, and names Murugan of Kurudimalai who rides the peacock to grind the northern peak to chaff, Kumara the guru, the sun to darkness.
613.nuance: The target is the patron-poet's trade: praising a man as Vishnu (கருடன் மிசைவரு கரிய புயல்), inserting his name (அவர்பெயர் செருகி), and stealing from older poems (திருடி ஒருபடி நெருடி). Whether 'I do not know their ways' is irony or confession is not said; the song has no explicit plea, which is unusual.

links.note: 15 confesses that the poet himself begged from patrons, praising them as clouds in giving; 613 looks at the same trade from outside, at poets who praise men as the cloud-dark Vishnu and steal verses, and disowns their way.
